practice_description.medium: Video game engines, interactive installation, animation, web-based archives, performance
practice_description.practice_summary: Danielle Brathwaite-Shirley creates interactive digital archives and game-like environments that center Black trans experience, treating archiving as a radical act of survival and challenging who controls the narratives and data of marginalized communities.
practice_description.methodology: Brathwaite-Shirley uses video game engines (primarily Unity) to build immersive, navigable environments that archive Black trans stories, histories, and experiences. The work is built through direct collaboration with Black trans people who contribute their stories, voices, and likenesses. The interactive format means visitors must make choices that implicate them in the archive -- asking whether they are an ally or not, and gating access to certain stories based on responses. The aesthetic draws on lo-fi game environments, glitch art, and DIY animation. The archival practice is explicitly political: it asks who gets to build archives, who is included or excluded, and what happens to data about marginalized people.

relevance_to_sense_room.relevance_summary: Brathwaite-Shirley's work fundamentally rethinks who governs identity data and how archives are structured -- directly relevant to A(DAI)'s concerns about commons infrastructure, data governance, and whose knowledge systems prevail. The interactive, choice-based navigation of her archives models a form of graph-like relational traversal.
relevance_to_sense_room.art_as_substrate: Partially -- the archives function as data substrates containing stories, voices, and images that could be embedded in larger systems. However, the work's politics would resist being absorbed into another system without careful attention to consent and governance.
relevance_to_sense_room.relational_composition: Yes -- the interactive archives are structured as branching, choice-based narratives where the visitor's path through the material is determined by their responses and relationships to the content. The archive's structure is relational: stories connect to other stories, identities to communities, histories to presents.
relevance_to_sense_room.self_recomposing: Partially -- the archives grow as new stories are contributed, and the interactive format means each visitor's experience is different based on their choices. However, the underlying structure is authored rather than algorithmically evolving.

works.title: WE ARE HERE BECAUSE OF THOSE THAT ARE NOT
works.description: Interactive web-based and installation archive of Black trans lives, built in a game engine. Visitors navigate a 3D environment, encountering stories, testimonies, and histories of Black trans people. The work gates access based on the visitor's declared relationship to the community -- allies and community members experience different paths.
works.relevance: Core example of how archival infrastructure can be designed as artwork, with governance embedded in the visitor experience. Directly models questions about who accesses what data and under what conditions.

works.title: Resurrection Land
works.description: Video game installation where players navigate a world built from Black trans archives. The game mechanics embed ethical choices about witnessing, allyship, and complicity. Shown at major institutions including Tate, Serpentine, and international biennials.
works.relevance: Demonstrates how game mechanics can encode governance and ethical frameworks. The 'resurrection' metaphor -- bringing archived lives into active presence -- resonates with A(DAI)'s interest in living, evolving knowledge systems.

works.title: SHE KEEPS ME DAMN ALIVE
works.description: Interactive installation combining game engine environments with physical arcade-style interfaces. Visitors physically interact with custom-built controllers to navigate archives of Black trans experience.
works.relevance: Bridges digital archives with physical embodied interaction, demonstrating how data archives can be experienced spatially and haptically rather than just visually.

protocol_art_resonance.protocol_art_summary: Brathwaite-Shirley designs archival systems where the rules of access, the structure of navigation, and the ethics of witnessing are built into the artwork itself. The interactive gating mechanism -- asking visitors to declare their relationship to the community before accessing certain stories -- is a governance protocol embedded in the creative experience.
protocol_art_resonance.system_designed: Interactive archival systems with built-in access governance based on visitor identity/allyship declaration. A model for community-controlled data archives where the archived community has agency over how their stories are accessed and by whom.

commons_orientation.licence_model: Unknown -- works are presented in institutional/gallery contexts; the archives themselves are not released as open data or open source [uncertain]
commons_orientation.commons_summary: Brathwaite-Shirley's practice is deeply commons-oriented in spirit -- building shared archives for a marginalized community, centering collective memory over individual property. However, the commons is specifically defined: it belongs to the Black trans community, not to everyone equally. This is a model of selective commons -- open to the community it serves, with gatekeeping mechanisms for those outside it. This challenges universalist open-access models.

governance_model.governance_detail: The artworks themselves contain governance mechanisms: visitors must declare their identity/allyship and are given different access paths based on their responses. The artist makes the overarching structural decisions, but the archived community members shape the content. This is a hybrid of solo artistic direction and community-participatory content creation with embedded audience-responsive governance.

consent_and_authorship.consent_approach: Contributors to the archives share their stories voluntarily and with knowledge of how they will be used. The work is built in direct relationship with Black trans communities. However, the specifics of formal consent frameworks (data agreements, withdrawal rights, etc.) are not publicly documented in detail. [uncertain]
consent_and_authorship.authorship_model: Collaborative -- Brathwaite-Shirley is the artist and system designer, but the content comes from community contributors who share their stories, voices, and likenesses. The artist designs the vessel; the community fills it with meaning.

liveness_and_duration.temporal_detail: The interactive archives respond to visitor input -- choices determine navigation paths and what content is revealed. Each experience is different based on the visitor's declared identity and choices. The archives can grow over time as new stories are contributed, making them durational in the sense of accumulating material.

data_materiality.data_sources: Stories, testimonies, voices, and likenesses of Black trans people contributed through direct collaboration. Historical research into Black trans history. The artist's own experience and community knowledge.
data_materiality.data_provenance: Community-contributed with consent -- stories are shared voluntarily by members of the Black trans community through direct relationship with the artist. The provenance is rooted in trust and community belonging rather than formal institutional data agreements. [uncertain]

embedding_space_relevance.embedding_summary: The work does not engage with embedding or latent spaces in a technical ML sense. The navigable 3D environments are hand-crafted in game engines rather than generated from neural networks. However, conceptually the branching archive structure creates a kind of semantic space that visitors traverse.
embedding_space_relevance.multimodal: Yes -- the archives span visual (3D environments, animation), sonic (voices, music), textual (stories, prompts), and interactive/haptic (physical controllers, choice-based navigation) modalities, though not unified through a technical embedding space.

exhibition_modality.spatial_description: Works are typically installed as immersive environments with large projections or screens, custom physical interfaces (arcade-style controllers, buttons), and spatial audio. The physical setup implicates the visitor's body -- they must stand, reach, press, and choose. Some works are also accessible as web-based experiences. Gallery environments are often darkened and theatrically lit to create an atmosphere of ritual or ceremony.

interoperability.composability: Low -- works are self-contained artistic experiences with specific political and ethical framings. The archives are not designed to be extracted, remixed, or used as inputs for other systems. The gatekeeping mechanisms actively resist unrestricted access.
interoperability.technical_openness: Closed -- works are built in Unity but not released as open source or forkable. The archives are accessible through exhibition or web interfaces but are not available as data or APIs. [uncertain]

technical_approach.stack: Unity game engine; 3D modeling and animation; custom physical interface fabrication (arcade controllers, buttons); web deployment (WebGL for browser-based versions); audio recording and production; lo-fi/glitch aesthetic processing

network_position.scene_affiliation: Black trans art and activism; Berlin digital art scene; London art scene (Slade School of Fine Art, where they studied); UK institutional circuit (Tate, Serpentine, Barbican); international biennials; game art; queer digital art; archival art practice
network_position.connections: Serpentine Arts Technologies (exhibited); Tate (exhibited); American Artist (shared concerns about data, identity, and power); Legacy Russell (glitch feminism discourse); Transgender archives and community organizations; broader UK/European digital art networks

potential_role_in_adai.role_detail: Brathwaite-Shirley's practice offers a crucial critical perspective for A(DAI): it asks who commons infrastructure actually serves, how access should be governed, and what happens when marginalized communities' data enters collective systems. Their work challenges universalist open-access assumptions and models selective, community-governed archives -- an essential counterpoint in A(DAI)'s governance design.
